record.title: FrontierCS 2 benchmarks whether coding agents can improve real computer-science research artifacts
record.summary: An Oct 21 preprint introduces FrontierCS 2, a benchmark in which coding agents work inside real research repositories after the paper's contribution is removed, with the original implementation serving as the reference. A separate judge returns development feedback while withholding its evaluator and held-out workloads; a pass requires beating the reference on every metric and workload. The authors report 12 evaluated model-and-harness systems, one run per task across 48 public tasks and 13 computer-science domains. Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code passed 58% of its runs; no agent passed on 16 tasks. The author repository says 48 of 150 planned tasks are public and lists 13 model entries, including Kimi K2.7 as the FCI zero point. These are benchmark-author results, not independent evidence of general research capability; model and harness effects are paired.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The preprint and author repository disclose a benchmark design built from real research artifacts: each task removes a paper contribution from its released code, gives the agent the repository and development feedback, and withholds the final evaluator and workloads. The pass criterion is to beat the human reference on every held-out workload and metric.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report 12 evaluated model-and-harness systems with one run per task over 48 public tasks spanning 13 computer-science domains. Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code passed 58% of its runs; no agent passed any of 16 tasks. These are single-run author-reported benchmark outcomes, not a repeatability estimate.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper pairs each model with one harness and settings, so the reported ranking does not isolate model weights from harness behavior. The author's repository lists 13 model entries across 48 tasks; it documents Kimi K2.7 as the zero point for the capability-index fit, reconciling that count with the 12 agents evaluated for pass outcomes.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent task replay, reference-parity check or audit of the full benchmark selection and scoring pipeline was performed in this review.
One run per task does not estimate run-to-run variance, and model identity is confounded with harness, reasoning settings and token limits.
The author repository says 48 of 150 planned tasks are public; performance on the remaining tasks and later releases is not established.

brief.importance_rationale: If the tasks and judging function as described, testing agents against real published systems across 13 computer-science areas could materially improve measurement of AI-assisted R&D capability and expose where benchmark scores fail to translate into complete engineering passes. Its single-run design and model-harness pairing narrow the conclusion.
limitations: The paper reports one run per task for each evaluated model-and-harness system; repeated-run reliability is unknown.
Each model is paired with a different harness and settings, so the leaderboard is not a model-only comparison.
The 58% result is from Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code on this benchmark and does not establish general autonomous research capability or superiority across other tasks.
The public benchmark contains 48 of 150 planned tasks; unseen-task and selection effects remain open.
No independent reproduction or validation of the authors' full task and judge pipeline was performed in this review.
brief.summary: An Oct 21 preprint introduces FrontierCS 2, a benchmark in which coding agents work inside real research repositories after the paper's contribution is removed, with the original implementation serving as the reference. A separate judge returns development feedback while withholding its evaluator and held-out workloads; a pass requires beating the reference on every metric and workload. The authors report 12 evaluated model-and-harness systems, one run per task across 48 public tasks and 13 computer-science domains. Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code passed 58% of its runs; no agent passed on 16 tasks. The author repository says 48 of 150 planned tasks are public and lists 13 model entries, including Kimi K2.7 as the FCI zero point. These are benchmark-author results, not independent evidence of general research capability; model and harness effects are paired.

technical.claimed_result: The paper reports 12 evaluated agents, each paired with one harness and run once per task across 48 public tasks in 13 domains. Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code passes 58% of its runs; every other agent passes fewer than half, and no agent passes on 16 tasks. The repository lists an additional model entry, Kimi K2.7, as the zero point for the FrontierCS Capabilities Index rather than one of the 12 agents used for pass-rate results.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint and author repository document the benchmark design, released task infrastructure, evaluation settings and reported run archive. the research desk did not execute a task or independently reproduce the results.
technical.mechanism: Each task starts from a published artifact repository with the paper's contribution removed. The agent edits and submits patches with allowed development-suite feedback; a separate judge keeps the evaluator, original reference and held-out workloads hidden. A pass requires beating the reference on every final metric and workload.
technical.regime: 48 publicly released tasks across 13 computer-science domains; 12 model-and-harness agents with one run per task; five-hour agent budgets per repository README. Results and cost-sensitive rankings depend on the task suite, harness, configuration and budget.
technical.strongest_baseline: The original published implementation retained as the human reference for each task, evaluated on the paper's workloads and held-out workloads.

brief.title: FrontierCS 2 benchmarks whether coding agents can improve real computer-science research artifacts
brief.why_it_matters: If its tasks and hidden evaluation behave as described, this benchmark measures whether agents can improve published systems under realistic repository, workload and cost constraints across a broad set of computer-science domains. It also makes a useful distinction between partial score gains and fully passing every held-out metric. The reported leaderboard remains a single run per task and pairs each model with one harness, so it does not isolate model-only capability or run-to-run reliability.
